insolent

/IN-suh-lent/ — stress on first syllable; rhymes with tolerant · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insolent describes behavior that is boldly rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone who is owed respect.

The insolent recruit rolled his eyes while the sergeant was speaking.

Example

A junior officer, openly insolent, glares at her commanding general and flatly contradicts his order in front of the assembled troops.

The officer's behavior is not just rude — it is boldly defiant toward someone she is supposed to respect and obey. Insolent captures that combination: open disrespect aimed deliberately at an authority figure. A plain word like 'rude' would miss the confrontational boldness and the violation of the power dynamic.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flippant: Flippant means treating a serious matter with careless, joking disrespect — a wisecrack during a fire drill. The flippant speaker may not mean to defy anyone at all. Insolent behavior is bolder and more pointed: open rudeness aimed at someone owed respect, a deliberate challenge rather than a careless joke.

defiant: Defiant means openly refusing to obey — digging in against an order, a rule, or an authority. Insolent describes the manner more than the refusal: boldly rude words, smirks, or eye-rolls aimed at someone owed respect. A defiant recruit won't follow the order; an insolent one mocks the sergeant while ignoring it.

cheeky: Cheeky means playfully bold in a small, usually forgivable way — a grin and a daring joke that skirts the rules. Insolent is far harsher: boldly rude and openly disrespectful toward someone owed respect. Cheekiness can make an adult smile; insolence is a challenge no teacher can let pass.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deferential: politely yielding to another's authority or wishes

reverent: showing deep, awed respect for someone

Where it sits · how openly someone defies authority

rude → disrespectful → insolent → contemptuous

rude vs. insolent: Rude is weaker than insolent: rude behavior is ordinary bad manners, while insolent behavior boldly defies someone who is owed respect.

disrespectful vs. insolent: Disrespectful is weaker than insolent; a disrespectful person fails to show proper respect, but an insolent person flaunts that failure openly and defiantly.

contemptuous vs. insolent: Contemptuous is stronger than insolent: insolent behavior boldly disrespects authority, while contemptuous behavior adds deep scorn, treating the person as beneath consideration entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: not, opposite of (Latin)

Root — sol (solere): to be accustomed, to be in the habit of (Latin)

Suffix — -ent: forming adjectives: doing or being (Latin)

Put it together: Insolent literally meant 'not according to custom' — behavior that breaks with what people are accustomed to. From there it came to describe conduct that boldly ignores the respect custom says someone is owed, especially a person in authority.

Use the root in a new word: obsolete: The floppy disk is now obsolete — people have 'grown out of the custom' of using it — built on the same Latin root solere, 'to be accustomed,' that makes insolent literally mean 'breaking with custom.'

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / standard

Insolent is stronger than rude because it emphasizes boldness and direct disrespect toward someone owed respect. Use it when someone openly defies or challenges authority. For mild, everyday rudeness, rude is simpler and better.
